controls.statement: Product behavior matches published privacy notices and user choices.
New data uses undergo privacy review.
Consent is used only where appropriate and is specific, informed, granular, recorded, and withdrawable.
Cookie, tracker, analytics, advertising, attribution, session-replay, and experimentation inventories match production behavior.
Third-party tools receive only approved data.
Sensitive fields are redacted from logs, monitoring, support tools, recordings, analytics, and error reports.
Requester verification is proportionate and does not collect excessive additional data.
Retention periods are explicit and enforced.
Deletion covers primary data, caches, indexes, derived data, exports, and downstream systems.
Pseudonymization and anonymization claims are validated.
Reidentification risk is assessed.
Data export cannot expose other users' or tenants' information.
Children's, biometric, health, precise-location, communications, financial, identity, and other sensitive data trigger enhanced review.
Processor and subprocessor contracts cover permitted use, security, deletion, assistance, audit, and incident notification.
A personal-data incident can be identified, scoped, contained, and reported within applicable deadlines.
Interfaces avoid manipulative consent, cancellation, and privacy choices.
Assign accountable privacy owners and data stewards for every product and processing purpose.
Maintain an inventory of personal data, sources, purposes, lawful basis or authorization, recipients, locations, retention, and deletion.
Map personal-data flows across clients, services, logs, analytics, support, suppliers, backups, models, and exports.
Apply privacy-protective defaults and collect only what is necessary for the stated purpose.
Separate mandatory processing from optional processing and communicate the difference.
Assess privacy risk before new collection, inference, combination, sharing, monitoring, or automated decision use.
Translate privacy principles into technical requirements, data models, access, retention, UI, telemetry, and tests.
Use purpose limitation and access controls to prevent unauthorized secondary use.
Minimize identifiers and linkability across contexts.
Use pseudonymization, aggregation, isolation, or on-device processing where they meaningfully reduce risk.
Include privacy threats such as reidentification, inference, surveillance, coercion, exclusion, and loss of autonomy.
Review suppliers for permitted use, location, retention, deletion, security, subprocessing, and incident duties.
Keep privacy records and notices consistent with deployed behavior.
Monitor data flows and trackers for unauthorized change.
Provide privacy review for high-risk processing and material product changes.
Treat privacy incidents and user complaints as design feedback.
Measure rights completion, deletion effectiveness, access minimization, unexpected collection, and risk reduction.
Train role-appropriate personnel before granting personal-data access.
Define privacy behavior through deprecation, migration, backup, and retirement.
Do not claim anonymization, consent, or compliance without evidence supporting the exact processing.
Describe what data is collected, why, from whom, how used, shared, retained, protected, and controlled.
Use concise contextual notice at the point of decision with access to complete detail.
Keep notice language accurate for actual production data flows and suppliers.
Distinguish required processing from optional analytics, personalization, advertising, sharing, or communication.
Use consent only when it is an appropriate legal and ethical basis.
Make consent specific, informed, unambiguous, granular, freely given, and recorded where required.
Do not bundle unrelated purposes or condition service on unnecessary consent.
Prevent nonessential processing before valid permission where required.
Make refusal and withdrawal as easy and understandable as acceptance.
Propagate preference changes promptly to all relevant systems, suppliers, caches, and future processing.
Define behavior for previously collected data after withdrawal.
Record notice version, purpose, choice, time, context, and proof without collecting excessive evidence.
Allow users to review and change preferences through an accessible interface.
Avoid manipulative hierarchy, preselection, repeated nagging, misleading toggles, or false necessity.
Test comprehension and operation with representative users and assistive technologies.
Re-consent only when purpose or processing materially changes and the basis requires it.
Avoid using inactivity as agreement.
Handle conflicting preferences across devices, accounts, organizations, and channels explicitly.
Monitor preference enforcement and investigate processing that contradicts user choice.
Retire obsolete consent records according to retention and audit needs.
Determine which rights and response timelines apply to each user, data category, and jurisdiction.

controls.statement: Define the intended threat model, recipients, data context, linkage sources, and acceptable reidentification risk.
Distinguish masking, tokenization, pseudonymization, aggregation, synthetic data, and anonymization accurately.
Do not treat removal of direct identifiers as sufficient anonymization.
Assess uniqueness, sparsity, rare combinations, free text, location, time, device, and behavioral linkage risk.
Minimize attributes and precision before applying complex transformation.
Keep reidentification keys separate, access-controlled, audited, and purpose-limited.
Use different pseudonyms across contexts when cross-context linkage is unnecessary.
Protect mappings and quasi-identifiers with controls appropriate to the original sensitivity.
Evaluate attacks using realistic auxiliary information and motivated recipients.
Measure utility and privacy together and document the trade-off.
Apply contractual and policy prohibitions on reidentification in addition to technical controls.
Review outputs, small groups, outliers, queries, and repeated releases for differencing risk.
Use privacy-preserving query controls, noise, thresholds, or aggregation where appropriate.
Validate synthetic data for memorization, leakage, bias, and unrealistic artifacts.
Reassess risk when new data sources, recipients, methods, or public information appear.
Avoid irreversible public release unless risk is demonstrably acceptable.
Label transformed data and permitted uses clearly.
Monitor misuse and downstream redistribution.
Delete or rotate mappings according to purpose and retention.
Make every anonymization claim bounded to context and supported by current evidence.
Inventory every destination country, provider, subprocessor, recipient, support location, backup region, and remote-access path.

controls.statement: Identify sensitive categories by jurisdiction, context, user expectation, harm, and inference—not labels alone.
Avoid collecting sensitive data unless it is necessary for a documented high-value purpose.
Use age-appropriate design and language when children may use or be affected by the service.
Determine age assurance, parental authorization, and child autonomy requirements proportionately.
Do not use dark patterns to encourage disclosure or extended engagement by children.
Disable unnecessary profiling, advertising, location, contact discovery, and public visibility by default for minors.
Protect biometric templates, health data, precise location, communications, identity documents, and financial data with enhanced access and encryption.
Avoid deriving sensitive traits from ordinary behavior unless explicitly justified and governed.
Limit retention and secondary use more strictly than ordinary data.
Prevent support, analytics, logs, and test systems from receiving unnecessary sensitive values.
Require independent review for new sensitive-data processing or sharing.
Provide meaningful alternatives where refusal is possible.
Design for family, guardian, school, employer, and joint-account conflicts without assuming one actor always represents the user.
Test disclosure, inference, enumeration, coercion, stalking, and account-recovery risks.
Provide rapid revocation, correction, deletion, and safety escalation.
Monitor for misuse, scraping, trafficking, discrimination, and harmful targeting.
Avoid public or permanent identifiers for minors and vulnerable users.
Use vendors with appropriate contractual and technical safeguards.
Review safety and privacy as users age or their legal status changes.
Stop processing when harm cannot be reduced below approved tolerance.
